Sebene

A party DJ application that locates the best part of each song in a 214-song Thanksgiving playlist from the timing of its synced lyrics, sequences the cuts along a five-part evening arc, and plays them through two alternating Spotify players with a handover designed so that no silence is heard between songs, while the host keeps live control.

Visit the site ↗How to useIn motion

01

Problem statement

A party playlist is long relative to a party, and most songs make the room wait for their strongest passage. The problem is acute in Congolese rumba and soukous, where the sebene, the guitar-led dance section, often begins three to five minutes into a song after long sung verses. Streaming services start every track at zero, carry no notion of where a song peaks, and their transitions frequently leave a second or more of silence while the next track buffers. A host who intervenes to skip or search does so in front of the dance floor, and the floor empties.

02

Contribution

Atalaku, named after the animator who shouts over the sebene in Congolese music, is an agent that reads the playlist, locates the best part of each song and orders the cuts along a Thanksgiving evening in five parts: Welcome in, Around the table, Warming the floor, Dance floor and Last dance. No artist returns within four songs and no style plays three times in a row. Playback alternates between two Spotify players so that each best part flows into the next. The host retains live control: Mix now, Ride this song past its cut, Jump to hot part, a tap anywhere on the record ring to seek, Start here to save a better moment for next time, heaters that drop one of the eight hottest unplayed songs in at once, and drag and drop of any song onto Next, onto Play now, or within the list of picks, which always precede the agent’s choices. A Soundcheck mode plays each estimated cut for 12 seconds for review, and a party screen presents the evening on a television. The 214 songs, which amount to 19 h 07 min of music, are reduced to about 3 h 30 min of best parts at the standard cut length.

03

Architecture

The system has three parts. A build-time agent in Node.js runs at every deployment on Vercel: it reads the crate, in which each song carries a style, an energy level from 2 to 5 and a popularity rank from 1 to 3 assigned by hand, queries LRCLIB for synced lyrics and Spotify’s oEmbed service for covers through five parallel workers with retries and back-off, and writes the analysed set as a static file. The client is a single page in plain JavaScript, about 870 lines with no framework, that performs sequencing, playback and the interface through the Spotify iFrame API; settings, cut corrections and added songs persist in the browser’s local storage. A serverless function analyses songs added after the build: it reads title, artists and length from Spotify’s public embed page, or receives them from the sync, and applies the same lyric lookup and cut logic to at most twelve songs per call. Playlist sync uses OAuth 2.0 with PKCE directly from the browser against the host’s own Spotify developer application, so no server holds a token. Transition sounds and the drum bridge are synthesized at run time with the Web Audio API, without audio samples.

04

Method and data

Lyric timing is used only when the lyric record’s duration lies within 4 s of the Spotify track. A refrain is the most repeated block of at least two consecutive lines, scored as block length, capped at eight lines, times the number of repetitions; the occurrence nearest the style’s usual chorus position is chosen and the cut starts 3 s before it, lasting the longer of the style’s cut length and the refrain span plus 14 s, up to 80 s. For rumba and soukous the sebene is the first line between 28% and 80% of the song where the median line length falls from five words or more over the previous eight lines to four or fewer over the next eight, with at least 40% of those lines repeated, which is the change from sung verses to the atalaku’s shouts; failing that, the first silence of at least 18 s in the singing within the same bounds. Remaining songs are placed by style profile, for example rumba at 50% of the song for 70 s, soukous at 42% for 65 s and afrobeats at 22% for 45 s, with adjustments for very short songs, long songs and the medley. The arc assigns songs to slots of a target energy curve by rank of energy plus 0.22 times popularity above one plus seeded noise, then a swapping pass enforces the spacing rules. In playback, the next cut is loaded on the idle player at its hot part about 15 s ahead and started 1.2 s before the current cut ends; the play command is sent only after the load is confirmed, waiting at most 1.5 s, and repeated every 0.45 s until sound is reported, because a command sent during a load is ignored or briefly resumes the previous song. The outgoing player stops only after the incoming one reports sound, plus the blend time. When neither player sounds while the party is on, a drum bridge at 118 beats per minute, built from synthesized kick, clap, hi-hat, shaker and toms, starts at once during a transition or after 0.7 s within a song, for at most 12 s, and the transition boom lands when the new song becomes audible.

05

Verification and limitations

A stand-in for the Spotify player reproduced the delays that cause gaps: a load time, commands ignored during a load, buffering before sound, one stream per account, songs that keep reporting buffering while they play, and update streams that fall silent. Driven in headless Chrome and sampled every 50 ms, the unbridged silence was 0 ms in every condition, and drag to Next and the reordering of picks behaved as specified. On the production site with real Spotify players, consecutive songs overlapped for about 2.5 s with no gap; that test revealed songs that report buffering while playing, which had set off the drum bridge over the music, and the fault was corrected. Limitations: the embedded players expose no volume control, so a blend is an overlap rather than a fade; full songs require the browser to be signed in to Spotify, otherwise 30-second previews play; 135 cuts are estimates intended for Soundcheck; corrections are stored in one browser and moved with Copy my fixes; automatic sync requires a Spotify developer application, which Spotify reserves for Premium accounts. Only line timings are used, and no lyric text is stored or displayed.
